ORIGINAL ARTICLE
Enhancing intra-aural disease classification with attention-based deep learning models
Furkancan Demircan1 • Murat Ekinci2 • Zafer Co ̈mert1,3
Received: 6 December 2023 / Accepted: 3 January 2025 / Published online: 21 January 2025  The Author(s) 2025
Abstract Ear diseases are defined as pathological conditions that indicate dysfunction or abnormal function of the ear organ, which is part of the auditory system of living organisms that regulates hearing and balance functions. These diseases usually manifest as conditions that affect the internal components of the ear structure and can manifest themselves with symptoms such as hearing loss, ear pain, balance problems, and fluid accumulation in the ear. The accuracy of the diagnosis depends on expert knowledge and subjective opinion. This method is prone to human error. This study presents a novel computer- aided diagnosis system for otoscope images of ear diseases, utilizing a vision transformer-based feature extractor combined with machine learning classifiers to provide accurate second opinions for ENT specialists. For this purpose, a new model based on state-of-the-art vision transformer feature extractor and machine learning models is proposed. In the experimental study, the dataset, comprising 880 eardrum images categorized into four classes (CSOM, earwax, myringosclerosis, and normal), was split into training (70%), validation (10%), and testing (20%) subsets. Each image was preprocessed to 420 9 380 pixels to fit the input dimensions of the models. The vision transformer architecture was utilized for feature extraction, followed by classification using various machine learning algorithms including kNN, SVM, and random forest. As a result, the model using vision transformer feature extractor and k-nearest neighbors (kNN) algorithm achieved 99.00% accuracy. In this study, a deep learning-based and computer-aided diagnosis system, in other words, a computational model, was developed instead of the current human error-prone disease diagnosis method used by ear nose throat (ENT) specialists. The main purpose of the deep learning-based decision support system is to support the diagnosis process where expert knowledge is difficult to access and to provide an alternative opinion to the expert diagnosis.
Keywords Classification  Ear diseases  Deep learning  Transformers  Machine learning
1 Introduction
Ear diseases, also known as otological disorders, refer to medical conditions that affect the structure and function of the ear. Ear diseases, which adversely affect people of all ages, cause various symptoms and complications if left untreated. Examples of these disorders include hearing loss, balance disorder, speech retardation, dizziness, nausea and ear pain. These conditions target different parts of the ear, including the outer, middle and inner ear. Common ear diseases in daily life include otitis media, otitis externa, tinnitus, hearing loss, Meniere’s disease and earwax effect [1].
Diagnosing ear diseases typically involves ENT spe- cialists examining the inside of the ear using an otoscope. This process, while effective, is highly dependent on the

expertise of the specialist and can be prone to human error. This study aims to enhance diagnostic accuracy by inte- grating advanced deep learning models with traditional machine learning classifiers to create a robust computer- aided diagnosis system. The diagnosis is based on expert knowledge, symptoms and response to the treatment pro- cess. In the guidelines published by the World Health Organization in March 2023, the ‘‘Wait and See Approach’’ is recommended for the patient before a definitive diagnosis is made [2]. This approach is the diagnosis of the disease as a result of long-term monitoring of the disease and the approach prevents misdiagnosis.
Leveraging clinical knowledge, patient data, and health information, clinical knowledge support systems (CKSS) are revolutionizing healthcare by optimizing diagnosis and treatment. These systems empower informed decision- making, mitigate medication errors through proactive identification of drug–drug interactions, expedite diagnoses with data-driven insights, and enhance efficiency by streamlining processes and reducing redundant tests. As CKSS continues to evolve and gain widespread adoption, it presents a future of improved patient safety, enhanced quality of care, and increased healthcare efficiency [3].
2 Literature review
Until this date, research on computer-aided clinical deci- sion support systems has been carried out in various aca- demic studies.
Wu et al. proposed a mobile application for easy mon- itoring and classification of pediatric otitis media using Xception and MobileNetV2 convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures pre-trained on ImageNet for back- ground classification. In the training and testing of the proposed method, it was applied on 12203 images con- taining three types of otitis media diseases obtained from Shenzhen Children’s Hospital between January 2016 and December 2019. As a result of the study, Xception and MobileNetV2 architectures achieved 97.82% and 96.04% accuracy in the test images on the system and 90.85% and 88.89% accuracy in the test images on the mobile appli- cation, respectively [4].
Sundgaard et al. proposed InceptionV3 architecture pre- trained on ImageNet to automatically diagnose otitis media in otoscope images. The proposed method was trained and tested on 1136 images of three types of otitis media from 519 patients at the Kamide ENT clinic in Shizuoka, Japan. Five different loss functions were compared in the study, and the best success was obtained from the triple loss function with an accuracy of 85% [5].
Alhudhaif et al. proposed a hybrid model based on CNN architecture to support the diagnosis of five types of otitis
media diseases. In the training and testing of the proposed architecture, an open-access dataset of 956 otoscope ima- ges from Private Van Akdamar Hospital between October 2018 and June 2019, which were classified into eight types of diseases by experts, was used. The decision mechanism of the CNN architecture was developed using a combina- tion of channel and spatial model (CBAM), residual blocks and hypercolumn technique. On the same dataset, AlexNet, VGG-16, VGG-19, GoogleNet, ResNet50 and the proposed method showed 81.40%, 81.40%, 84.88%, 80.23%, 80.23%, 80.23% and 98.26% accuracy for four classes, respectively [6].
Tran et al. proposed an automatic diagnostic system for pediatric otitis media images using a level set based active counter method for segmentation, color, HOG and SSIM features for feature extraction and joint sparse representa- tion algorithm for disease classification. For training and testing of the proposed method, 1230 digital otoscope images of children in General Cathay Hospital were used, which were diagnosed by experts under two types of dis- eases. The proposed method showed 91.41% accuracy on the test dataset [7].
Myburgh et al. proposed a mobile application that uses cloud-based decision trees and neural network structure to automatically diagnose five types of otitis media diseases. In the training and testing of the proposed method, 562 video otoscope images containing five types of otitis media diseases obtained from different sources were used. The proposed decision tree and neural network showed 81.58% and 86.84% accuracy, respectively [8].
Mohammed et al. proposed a system that can automat- ically diagnose otitis media using CNN-EfficientNetB0 feature extractor, Bayesian optimization hyperparameter selector and CNN-BiLSTM classifier. The combination of CNN-BiLSTM architectures showed higher performance and worked faster than the methods based on CNN archi- tecture alone. In the training and testing of the proposed method, 880 otoscope images with four types of diseases obtained from the Department of Otorhinolaryngology of the Clinical Hospital of Universidad de Chile were used. The proposed architecture showed 100% accuracy [9].
Uc ̧ar et al. proposed to classify the images of otitis media disease by feeding the hyperparameters obtained from five different layers to the BiLSTM network by feeding SURF keypoints to the VGG-16 architecture. In the training and testing of the proposed architecture, 880 images from the Department of Otorhinolaryngology of the Clinical Hospital of Universidad de Chile were used. Using SURF, keypoints were obtained, and the system was made independent of the color space thanks to the keypoints. The proposed architecture showed an average accuracy of 99.06% [10].

Wang et al. proposed the MESIC architecture for clas- sifying intra-ear diseases. The dataset consists of a total of 998 images of three classes obtained from CT scans of patients in Xiangya Hospital. Before using the images in the proposed architecture, preprocessing is performed. In the preprocessing, a region of interest with a size of 100 9 100 pixels is extracted. In the proposed architecture, features are extracted from the images with the VGG-16 model. From the extracted features, three new feature maps are obtained with the attention block. Full-connected layer and softmax are used to classify the feature maps. The proposed architecture showed 90.1% accuracy on the dataset [11].
Cha et al. compared the classification performance of different models for automatic diagnosis of ear diseases. The dataset was 10544 otoendoscopic images of six classes obtained from patients at Severance Hospital. The images are divided into 80% and 20% to be used for training and testing, respectively. AlexNet, GoogLeNet, ResNet, InceptionV3, Inception-ResNetV2, SqueezeNet and MobileNetV2 were selected from open deep learning models. As a result of the application of the dataset on the models, the two models with the highest success were selected. A probability selector is proposed that combines the outputs of the two models. The probability selector classifies the image according to the label with the highest score from the two models. As a result of the study, the proposed model shows 93.67% accuracy [12].
Chen et al. proposed an AI-assisted mobile algorithm that can classify diseases inside the ear. As a dataset, 2161 images of ten classes obtained from Taipei Veteran Gen- eral Hospital were used. The images are divided into 80% and 20% for training and testing, respectively. ‘‘Augmen- tation’’ was applied to the images as preprocessing. VGG19, VGG19, Xception, InceptionV3, NASNetLarge and ResNet50 were selected as deep learning models. The feature maps of the models were extracted using CAM (class activation map). The InceptionV3 model showed the highest accuracy with 98%. The weight values obtained from the InceptionV3 model were given to the NasNet- Mobile, MobileNetV2 and DenseNet201 models for use in the mobile system. At the end of this study, the highest success rate for the mobile system was obtained from the MobileNetV2 model with 97.6%. The proposed study shows that the mobile system can diagnose as successfully as experts [13].
Sundgaard et al. proposed an architecture that uses broadband tympanometry (WBT) signal values to classify otitis media. Broadband tympanometry measures the acoustic properties of the ear canal using frequency signals. The healthy ear canal showed higher absorption values than the diseased one. In the study, 1014 WBT measure- ments obtained from patients aged 2 months to 12 years at
the Kamide ENT clinic in Japan were used as the data set. The measurements were performed using the Titan system. Three classes of data were obtained: 488 healthy (NOE), 372 OME and 154 AOM. The data set was divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing, and the training data set was again divided into 20% and used for validation. First, a model inspired by the AlexNet architecture is proposed for two classes (healthy and OM). The proposed model is compared with the pre-trained VGG, ResNet and InceptionV3 available in the PyTorch library. Since the pre-trained models are trained image-based, their accuracy is low. The accuracy of the proposed model is 92.6%. In the second approach, OM disease was tried to be differ- entiated but could not be differentiated [14].
Tsutsumi et al. proposed a web-based deep learning model for automatic classification of ear diseases. The dataset used in the study was a combination of images available on the internet and Google Image images. The dataset consists of 400 images, including 116 AOM, 44 otitis externa, 23 CSOM, and 21 earwax impaction. The dataset is divided into two different classes, categorical and dichotomous. The dataset was divided into 75% for train- ing and 25% for testing. CNN architectures ResNet50, InceptionV3, InceptionResNetV2 and MobileNetV2 were selected for classification. As a result of the study, the highest accuracy success for the binary class was obtained from the MobileNetV2 model with 90%. For the categor- ical class, the MobileNetV2 model achieved 91% accuracy [15].
Wang et al. proposed a deep learning model using CT images for COM disease detection. Images from 672 CT scans of 562 patients were used as the dataset. The images were obtained from a 128-channel multi-detector SOMA- TOM Definition Edge CT scanner. The axial view of the temporal bone allowed both ears to be included in the images, resulting in a total of 1344 ear images. After the two ears were examined by experts, a final dataset of 1147 images belonging to three classes, namely CSOM, normal and cholesteatoma, was extracted. In the dataset, 85% of the images were used for training and validation and 15% for testing. Faster R-CNN model was used to extract the ear region in the dataset. The number of images was increased by applying augmentation to the images in the dataset. InceptionV3 model was used for feature extraction, and softmax function was used for classification. The perfor- mances of the proposed model and six experts on the test data are compared. The average accuracy of the proposed model on two classes (CSOM and Normal) is 86%. The average accuracy of the experts is 82% [16].
Zeng et al. investigated the potential of deep learning (DL) for identifying key features of otitis media with effusion (OME), a middle ear infection. Within the scope of the study, a data set consisting of 6393 images was used.

Their study focused on detecting atelectasis (collapsed tissue) and attic retraction pocket (a specific indentation) in otoscopic images (ear canal images) collected from mul- tiple centers. The researchers developed and validated a DL model (InceptionV3 with CAM) that achieved high accuracy in detecting both features, with 89% accuracy for attic retraction and 79% accuracy for atelectasis. Notably, the model also highlighted the most relevant image regions for identifying these features [17].
In a study exploring the generalizability of deep learning for ear disease detection, Habib et al. investigated how well these algorithms performed on images from different locations. They used a dataset of over 1800 otoscopic images collected across diverse geographic regions: Van (Turkey), Santiago (Chile), and Ohio (USA). The images were classified as normal or abnormal using four deep learning models: ResNet50, DenseNet-161, VGG16, and vision transformer. A technique called fivefold cross-vali- dation was employed to assess the models’ performance on both the original dataset and unseen external images. The highest accuracy value of 92% was obtained from the vision transformer model. While the algorithms achieved high accuracy when tested on the initial dataset (internal images), their performance dropped significantly when evaluated on external images from new locations [18].
In a 2021 study, Pham et al. proposed a novel deep learning approach called EAR-UNet. This model tackles the challenge of segmenting tympanic membranes from otoscopic images. Built upon the foundation of the UNet architecture, EAR-UNet leverages three key components: EfficientNet for efficient feature extraction in the encoder, an attention gate for improved information flow in the skip connections, and residual blocks within the decoder to enhance feature learning. To assess its performance, the researchers evaluated EAR-UNet on a dataset containing otoscopic images from 1024 patients, both diagnosed with and without otitis media. Notably, the model achieved an impressive average dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.929, demonstrating its effectiveness in segmentation without requiring additional preprocessing or post-pro- cessing steps [19].
Mesellem et al. developed a comparative model to evaluate the efficiency of various computational intelli- gence techniques for predicting dynamic adsorption of organic pollutants on activated carbon. Using a compre- hensive dataset of 11,763 data points, they tested five distinct models: ANN with conventional transfer functions, an ANN enhanced by the new SPOCU transfer function, SVM, a hybrid SVM with dragonfly optimization (SVM- DA), and ANFIS. The study found that the SVM-DA model was superior, achieving the highest accuracy with an RMSE of 0.037 and an R-value of 0.99, demonstrating the model’s robustness in diverse operational conditions [20].
Talaat et al. proposed an innovative approach to retinal disease diagnosis using an Attention-Based DenseNet model, incorporating an attention mechanism to focus on relevant OCT image features, enhancing diagnostic preci- sion. Using a dataset of 84,495 OCT images categorized into NORMAL, CNV, DME, and DRUSEN, the model achieved a validation accuracy of 91.67% and an impres- sive test accuracy of 95.83% after applying L2 regular- ization. These results underscore the model’s potential for high reliability and clinical applicability in retinal diag- nostics [21].
Machacuay et al. proposed the ShallowLSTM model for improved long-term indoor temperature predictions in refrigeration systems by modifying the LSTM structure with shallow neural networks. Their model was trained on five days of data from an experimental refrigeration plant, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0762 on a 120-min prediction horizon, outperforming standard LSTM models with a MAE of 0.2149. This improvement high- lights the ShallowLSTM’s capacity to handle longer pre- diction horizons effectively with fewer parameters [22].
Co ̈mert et al. proposed a computerized otoscopy image- based AI model for diagnosing otitis media (OM). The dataset used consisted of 880 otoscope images from a publicly available Ear Imagery dataset, categorized into four classes: chronic otitis media, myringosclerosis, earwax plug, and normal conditions. The method involved using vision transformers (ViT) for deep feature extraction, combined with support vector machines (SVM) optimized through grid search. The best-performing model, optimiz- able SVM, achieved an accuracy of 99.37%, showcasing exceptional classification performance [23].
While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrably achieved success in ear disease classification tasks within past research, there is a lack of exploration into the potential of transformer-based classifier models, currently recognized as the cutting edge in deep learning. To fill this gap in the literature, this study aims to develop an ear disease classifier model using the vision transformer architecture. To improve the performance of the vision transformer model, hybrid classifiers with machine learn- ing algorithms are proposed in the study.
3 Material and method
In the ever-evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning have emerged as transformative forces. Machine learning algorithms, the workhorses of this revolution, equip computers with the ability to learn from data, a cornerstone of human intelli- gence. By analyzing massive datasets, these algorithms uncover hidden patterns and make increasingly accurate

predictions. Deep learning, a more advanced subfield, takes inspiration from the structure and function of the human brain. These sophisticated models achieve even greater feats of learning and problem-solving, mimicking the neural networks that power human cognition. Both machine learning and deep learning offer a multitude of advantages, automating tasks, extracting valuable insights from data, and paving the way for groundbreaking advancements across numerous fields. These powerful tools leverage data to make predictions, decisions, or classifications. However, understanding the specific strengths and limitations of both approaches is crucial for harnessing their full potential.
One crucial limitation of machine learning algorithms lies in their dependency on extensive amounts of labeled data for effective training. While these data enable algo- rithms to identify patterns and make accurate predictions, acquiring and labeling it can be time-consuming and expensive, particularly in specialized domains that require expert knowledge. This dependency is generally seen as a disadvantage because it creates a significant barrier to entry, making the process prohibitively costly and slow for many applications. Moreover, the quality of the training data directly affects model performance, adding another layer of complexity and potential cost. Additionally, these algorithms often require feature engineering, a labor-in- tensive process where domain experts manually extract relevant characteristics from raw data to improve model accuracy. Deep learning models, while powerful, demand significant computational resources like GPUs and vast memory, limiting their accessibility. They are also prone to overfitting, where the model performs well on training data but poorly on new, unseen data.
This study aims to design a model for classifying images of ear diseases by combining the advantages of machine learning and deep learning models. The state-of-the-art vision transformer architecture, known for its effectiveness in deep learning, has been chosen as the foundation for the deep learning model. Commonly used machine learning algorithms have been selected for the machine learning model. The schematic diagram of the conducted study is presented in Fig. 1.
First, input images are fed into the pre-trained vision transformer for feature extraction. The final classification layers are then removed, and the remaining model’s weights are frozen to preserve learned features. This allows the model to extract informative feature maps from the input images. Global average pooling reduces the dimen- sionality of these feature maps into one-dimensional vec- tors. Finally, these vectors are fed into commonly used machine learning algorithms for classification. The model with the highest accuracy is then compared against
traditional CNN-based models to assess their overall clas- sification performance.
3.1 Dataset
Within the scope of the study, Ear Imagery dataset with ear diseases was used. This dataset contains eardrum images of 180 patients obtained from the ENT department of the Clinical Hospital of Universidad de Chile. The images were obtained from the left and right ear and were cate- gorized into four classes as CSOM, earwax, myringoscle- rosis and normal after being examined by experts [24]. The categorical classification of images related to ear diseases is based on the diagnoses made by experts, taking into account the structural abnormalities in the eardrum. The images are 420 9 380 pixels in size and in JPG format. The dataset consists of 880 images in total, 220 images for each class. Figure 2 shows examples of the images in the dataset.
3.2 Preprocessing
In the preprocessing step, the images in the dataset were resized according to the input dimensions of the models of interest. The images obtained as a result of the resizing were divided into 70%, 10% and 20% for training, vali- dation and testing, respectively. The created datasets con- tain 616, 88, 176 images, respectively.
3.3 Proposed model
3.3.1 Backbone
As the backbone network model, the vision transformer model, which is considered state-of-the-art today, was chosen. The vision transformer architecture was first introduced by Dosovitskiy et al. in 2020. Unlike traditional convolutional neural networks (CNN), the architecture utilizes the Transformer layers used in NLP processes in computer vision tasks.
The basic components of the vision transformer model are image rectification, linear estimation, spatial coding, transformer coding and the classifier head. Image rectifi- cation decomposes the input image into non-intersecting fixed-size segments. In linear estimation, the segment placements are linearly mapped to a set of symbols. In spatial coding, spatial coding information is added to the segment embeddings to capture spatial information. In transfer coding, fragment embeddings and their spatial encodings are processed from stacked transformer layers. The self-attention mechanism allows the model to capture long-term dependencies in the data. Classification is per- formed by outputting the last transformer layer to the

The multi-head attention mechanism is a neural network that allows the model to attend simultaneously to different parts of the input image. The mechanism first decomposes the input image into multiple parts. Each head participates in the input sequence using a scaled dot product attention mechanism. The outputs from each head are combined and passed through the linear layer in the multi-head attention mechanism to obtain the feature map. The mathematical formulation of the attention mechanism is given in Eq. (1). The query, key and value matrices obtained from each part are used to calculate the attention mechanism.

The attention mechanism increases the weight values of the parts with relevant elements and decreases the weight values of the parts without elements. As a result of this

the representation of the attributes of the item. In the rel- evance scoring process, the attention score is calculated using the inner product between the query and key vectors of a pair of items. The softmax function is then used to obtain the attention weights. The calculated attention scores are passed through the softmax function and prob- abilities are calculated. These probabilities represent the attention weights assigned to each item. In the last step, weighted value summation is performed. The attention weights obtained from the softmax function are used to calculate the weighted sum of all items multiplied by their value vectors. This weighted sum represents the attention- based representation of the input [25].
3.3.2 Classification head
In deep learning, the classification head is the last layer or set of layers that the neural network uses to predict output classes or categories. This layer predicts the output classes or categories using the feature maps obtained from the previous layers. In general, CNN models perform classifi- cation using fully connected layers.
Classification algorithms were used as the classification head. Classification algorithms are a fundamental part of machine learning and data analysis. They are used to classify data into predefined classes or categories based on certain characteristics or attributes. The main goal of classification algorithms is to predict unseen data with the learning obtained using seen data. In this study, k-nearest neighbors (kNN), support vector machine (SVM), Naive Bayes, decision tree, random forest, logistic regression and gradient boosting algorithms were used.
The kNN algorithm is a simple and intuitive machine learning algorithm used for both classification and regres- sion tasks. The classification process consists of four steps: training, prediction, voting and re-voting. The operations of the steps are as follows. All data points and their labels are stored in memory. Find k-nearest data points for the new data point based on distance. The number of occurrences of each class for k-nearest neighbors is calculated. The new data point is assigned the most frequent class among its k- nearest neighbors. These points influence the position and ori- entation of the hyperplane. The SVM algorithm uses the kernel trick for non-plane decompositions. The kernel trick involves transforming the data into a higher dimensional space. Equation (6) gives the mathematical formulation used for hyperplane calculation [26].

The classification process is completed by labeling each data point with the class it represents. In conclusion, SVM excels as a versatile classification algorithm by finding the optimal hyperplane that maximizes class separation. It maintains robustness even in complex scenarios with high dimensionality and nonlinear data.
The Naive Bayes algorithm is a probabilistic classifi- cation algorithm based on Bayes’ theorem. In essence, it uses Bayes’ theorem to calculate the probability of a given event based on prior knowledge of the relevant conditions. The algorithm works by assuming that the features for given class labels are independent of each other. This assumption significantly simplifies the calculation of probabilities in Bayes’ theorem [26].
Bayes’ theorem is a fundamental concept in probability theory. It relates conditional probabilities to marginal probabilities. It offers a framework for understanding the relationship between conditional probabilities and marginal probabilities. Conditional probability represents the likeli- hood of one event occurring, given the knowledge that another event has already taken place. In contrast, marginal probability reflects the overall probability of an event occurring without any dependence on other events. Bayes’ theorem bridges the gap between these two concepts, enabling us to re-evaluate our understanding of the prob- ability of an event when we gain new information or evi- dence. The mathematical formulation of the theorem is given in Eq. (10) [26].

Equation (12) gives the formula used to find the final probability by comparing the probabilities [26]. The win- ning class, so to speak, is the one with the highest proba- bility. However, in some instances, the probabilities for all classes might be equal. This scenario indicates that the classifier perceives all classes as equally likely for that specific input. This often happens when the observed fea- tures in the input data do not provide enough information to distinguish one class from another.
In the event of a tie in classification, several methods can be employed to break the deadlock and achieve a definitive outcome. One approach is random selection, which involves randomly choosing one of the equally probable classes. This method eliminates systematic bias and ensures equal treatment of all classes when the clas- sifier is unable to make a clear distinction. Although ran- dom selection is simple and effective, it lacks specific reasoning or prioritization. Alternatively, prior knowledge can be used to make a more informed decision. If a par- ticular class is known to be more critical or prevalent, it may be prioritized. Utilizing domain knowledge allows for more logical and effective decisions in specific scenarios, particularly when a certain class holds higher priority. For instance, in medical diagnosis, prioritizing a false positive for a critical illness over a false positive for a less serious condition can be crucial. Another refined solution involves employing a secondary criterion to differentiate classes. This could involve applying a different model, evaluating additional features, or integrating a specific heuristic approach. For example, using the outputs from a secondary model can assist in class separation. Additionally, includ- ing features not considered in the original model might provide clearer distinctions between the existing classes. This method represents a more complex and data-driven approach that can contribute to improved accuracy. By employing these methods, ties in model decisions can be effectively resolved, leading to more accurate classifications.

The decision tree algorithm is a flowchart-like structure where each internal node represents a feature, each branch represents a decision rule, and each leaf node represents the result. The root node represents the most important feature in the data. The internal nodes represent the features on which a decision is made. Branches from a node represent possible values or outcomes of the feature. Leaf nodes are the final output or decisions generated from the features. Decision trees can handle both numerical and categorical data. They also form the basis of random forest and gra- dient boosting algorithms [26].
The random forest algorithm uses groups of decision trees to make a more accurate and stable forecast. The random forest algorithm consists of decision trees, each of which produces its own prediction. When splitting a node in a tree, it only considers random subsets of features instead of considering all features. This adds diversity to the algorithm. In classification problems, the results pro- duced by the trees are counted, and the class with the most votes is the final prediction. The input vector for the training data D is given in Eq. Logistic regression is a probability-based classification algorithm. The algorithm uses the logistic function to model the relationship between features and the probability that the sample belongs to a particular class. The logistic regression algorithm models the relationship between the feature and the predicted probabilities using a sigmoid function. Normally, the algorithm is used for binary problems. With one-vs-rest (OvR) or softmax regression, the algorithm can also be used for multi-class problems [26].
The core of the logistic regression algorithm is the sigmoid function. The sigmoid function converts real-val- ued input features into outputs between (0, 1). The calcu- lation of the sigmoid function is given in Eqs. (15) and (16) [26].

Gradient boosting is a machine learning boosting algo- rithm used for classification and regression tasks. Boosting is a type of ensemble learning method that trains the model sequentially, and each new model corrects the output of the previous model. In this respect, the algorithm works dif- ferently from the random forest algorithm. It combines weak learners with strong learners. Here, weak learners are the models in the early stages of the algorithm. The output of these models is slightly better than random guessing. The main idea of the model is to combine the strengths of multiple models to obtain a model that outperforms the baseline models. The main goal of the algorithm is to minimize the loss function [19].
3.3.3 Performance metrics
Average precision and recall metrics, which are commonly used in object recognition tasks, are our performance measures in model evaluation (Bas ̧aran et al., 2020). In the classification process, general measurement values were obtained from the confusion (error) matrix consisting of true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN) and true negative (TN). The formulation of the measure- ment values, in other words, the performance criteria, is calculated with the help of the indices in the error matrix as expressed in Eqs. (18) to (21) [6].
Accuracy 1⁄4 TP þ TN TP þ FP þ FN þ TN ð18Þ
Recall 1⁄4 TP TP þ FN ð19Þ
Precision 1⁄4 TN TN þ FP ð20Þ
F  Skor 1⁄4 2  TP 2  TP þ FP þ TN ð21Þ
In the classification process, TP and TN correspond to correctly identified, and FP and FN to misidentified dis- eased and healthy eardrum images. The sensitivity metric is a measure of how well the model can detect positive examples. This metric is known as the true positive rate (TPR). This metric needs to be high for the model to classify correctly. The specificity metric, on the other hand, calculates the correct negative classification rates of the models. This metric is called the true negative rate (TNR).

4 Results
The computational framework for this study leveraged a powerful desktop computer equipped with an Intel i9- 13900 k processor and an NVIDIA RTX 4080 16 GB graphics card. To maximize the processing capabilities, the CUDA toolkit was employed, enabling utilization of the graphics card’s computational power. Core machine learning algorithms were implemented using the scikit- learn (Sklearn) library within the Python programming environment. This choice provided a robust and efficient foundation for traditional machine learning tasks. For tasks requiring deep learning capabilities, the PyTorch frame- work was employed, offering a flexible and powerful platform for building and training complex neural networks.
The decision to allocate 70% of the dataset for training, 10% for validation and 20% for testing resulted from several considerations in the context of ear disease classi- fication using transformer-based machine learning models. Initially, a 70% training subset was considered sufficient for the model to effectively learn the underlying patterns and features of ear diseases. This significant portion of the dataset facilitated a robust generalization of the model to unseen data during the training phase. It was then necessary to include a validation subset of 10% to fine-tune the hyperparameters and monitor the performance of the model during training. This subset helps to reduce overfitting by providing a separate dataset to which the model is not exposed during training and allows for a more accurate assessment of the model’s generalization capabilities. Finally, the remaining 20% of the dataset is reserved for testing purposes, serving as an independent benchmark to objectively evaluate the final performance of the trained model. This subset provides an unbiased assessment of the ability of the model to classify ear diseases on unseen data. While these partitioning ratios were chosen based on sound logic, it should be noted that there is no universally applicable rule for determining these ratios. Each dataset and problem domain has specific characteristics and goals.
The pre-trained vision transformer model was proposed as the backbone network of the developed model. The classification layers of the model were extracted and the feature maps obtained were saved in csv format. Machine learning models were used to classify the saved feature maps.
In the experimental study, different machine learning models were preferred for the classification process. These
models are kNN, SVM, decision tree, logistic regression, random forest, Naive Bayes and gradient boosting algo- rithm. In the training phase, epoch 50, batch size 32, learning coefficient 0.0001, momentum 0.2 and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) as the optimization algorithm was selected.

After the 35th epoch in the training phase, the graph curve flattened. This indicates that the model has completed its training. The validation graph showed similar characteristics to the training graph. This shows that the model was able to correctly classify the diseases in the blind dataset.

As seen in Table 1, the highest accuracy value was obtained from the KNN classification head with 99%. The developed architecture achieved 99% success in precision, recall and F1-score metrics. Figure 8 shows the ROC curve and AUC value for each class of the KNN classifier. In a detailed analysis of its performance, the model achieved exceptional results across all four ear conditions evaluated. For both ‘‘earwax’’ and ‘‘myringosclerosis,’’ the model boasts a perfect area under the curve (AUC) score of 1.0. This metric signifies the model’s flawless ability to classify these conditions, achieving perfect differentiation between them and healthy ears without any errors (either false positives or false negatives). This aggregated metric underscores the model’s exceptional ability to perform consistently well across the entire spectrum of analyzed ear

By leveraging the vision transformer for feature extraction and integrating it with various traditional machine learning classifiers such as kNN, SVM, and random forest, we achieved significant improvements in classification accuracy. This hybrid approach highlights the complementary strengths of deep learning and traditional machine learning techniques. The
vision transformer excels in capturing intricate patterns within the eardrum images, while the classifiers effectively distinguish between the four classes of ear diseases. Our results, particularly the 99% accuracy achieved by com- bining the vision transformer with kNN, underscore the potential of such integrative methodologies. This approach not only bridges the gap between classified models and featured ones, but also sets a new benchmark for the effi- cacy of medical image classification systems. In this respect, this study is different from previous studies. CNN- based models were proposed in previous studies, and Mohammed et al. achieved 100% classification success in their study. The ViT feature extractor and kNN classifier model used in this study achieved similar success values. The dataset used in the previous study was divided into 90% and 10% for training and testing steps, respectively. In this study, the dataset for training, validation and testing steps was split to 70%, 10% and 20%, respectively. Choosing the data split ratio is a crucial step in deep learning experiments, and a one-size-fits-all answer does not exist. For this purpose, the data split ratio was chosen considering the number of images in the dataset and ensuring sufficient data for model training and testing. Different ratios of sub-datasets were tested, and no sig- nificant change in the success rate was observed. The ViT- based model trained on the split dataset showed accuracy comparable to the previously proposed CNN-based models.

6 Conclusion
This study introduces a novel transformer-based model that combines the vision transformer (ViT) architecture with the k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classifier to enhance the accuracy of ear disease classification. Our findings demonstrate the significant potential of transformer models in medical imaging; specifically, the proposed model achieved a classification accuracy of 99%, which is notably higher than that of conventional convolutional neural net- work (CNN)-based models evaluated under identical

The ViT-kNN combination outperformed alternative machine learning algorithms across all assessed metrics, attaining superior performance in precision, recall, and F1-score, each reaching 99%. The model’s reliability was further validated through receiver operating charac- teristic (ROC) and area under the curve (AUC) analyses, where it exhibited near-perfect differentiation between disease states.
By automating feature extraction and classification, the proposed model addresses common diagnostic challenges such as human error and inter-observer variability, pro- viding otolaryngologists (ENT specialists) with a robust decision support tool that meets clinical needs for accurate second opinions. Our results indicate that transformer models, when integrated with traditional machine learning classifiers, can bridge the gap between advanced image recognition capabilities and the nuanced classification requirements inherent in medical diagnostics. To build upon these findings, future research should consider diversifying the dataset to include a broader range of ear disease types and otoscopic image sources, thereby enhancing the model’s versatility across different clinical settings. Additionally, developing a mobile application that integrates this model would facilitate wider accessibility, enabling on-site diagnostics in remote areas. Incorporating patient history and demographic information could further refine diagnostic accuracy, allowing for personalized treatment approaches. Collectively, these advancements pave the way for the implementation of AI-driven tools in routine ENT diagnostics, promoting broader access to accurate and efficient healthcare solutions.
